subtype: Approach: relying on the phone number memorised at home [Action]
passage: At the Nanded bus station, Samir lost sight of his father's white cap in the crowd of passengers. His knees were shaking. He walked to the information counter, where a woman named Seema was reading a register. "Please... my father's number," he said. Then the tune started in his head, the one he and his sister had sung in the kitchen for two weeks, and the digits rode along with it. He sang it under his breath and said each number out loud. Seema dialled as he spoke. In less than a minute a voice answered, and Samir let out a long breath.

qa.q: How had Samir practised his father's number?
qa.a: He had practised it as a tune that he and his sister sang in the kitchen for two weeks.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling as he stood at the counter, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was frightened, since his knees were shaking, and then relieved when a voice answered and he let out a long breath. 🙂

qa.q: What could Samir add to be extra ready next time, and why?
qa.a: He could also keep the number written on a card in his pocket, in case nerves make the tune slip.

qa.q: How does Seema see the way Samir gives the number?
qa.a: Seema hears each digit said clearly in order, so she can dial straight away and the call connects in under a minute.

grounding: A child who practised his father's number as a song recites it correctly at the information counter, despite shaking.

subtype: Approach: checking the rule that adults ask adults [Thinking]
passage: Wednesday. Something strange happened outside the tuition class today. A man in a grey car rolled down his window and said his puppy had run off, and asked me to sit in the car and help look for it. I stood still. In my head I said: when grown-ups need help finding something, they ask other grown-ups. They don't pick a kid. That is odd. Odd means careful. I said no thank you, walked backwards to the tuition gate and told Saurabh Sir straight away. He wrote down the colour of the car and said he would call Papa and tell the school today. My hands were shaking a bit after. - Hemant

qa.q: What did the man say had run off?
qa.a: He said his puppy had run off.

qa.q: What did Hemant think about the man's request?
qa.a: Hemant found it odd and decided it called for care, because grown-ups normally ask other grown-ups for help.

qa.q: What could Hemant do if no teacher had been nearby, and why?
qa.a: Hemant could walk to a busy shop or a group of adults, say what happened and ask them to call Hemant's parents, since a place with many people is safer than staying near the car.

qa.q: How might Saurabh Sir see Hemant's report?
qa.a: Saurabh Sir takes it seriously, writes down the car colour and passes it on the same day, seeing a child who did the right thing.

grounding: A child thinks that adults usually ask adults for help, finds the request odd, refuses and tells a teacher.

subtype: Approach: saying no and walking to a trusted adult [Action]
passage: Come closer, little one; your grandfather Tenzin wants to tell you what your cousin Trisha did when she was ten. A man near the school gate told her to come with him to see something. Trisha said, "No." She stepped back, kept a scooter's length away, and walked over to the security guard near the entrance. She told the guard exactly what the man had said, and the guard stood beside her until the man had gone. That evening she told her parents too, and we all sat and listened until she had finished. I was proud, but even more than that, I was relieved.

qa.q: Who did Trisha tell at the gate?
qa.a: Trisha told the guard at the gate.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when he heard about that evening?
qa.a: He felt proud and even more relieved that Trisha was safe.

qa.q: What choices did Trisha make that kept her safe?
qa.a: She said no, kept her distance and walked to the guard, then told her parents, so adults knew straight away.

qa.q: How might the guard have seen Trisha coming toward him?
qa.a: The guard probably saw a child asking for protection, and stood beside her until the man had gone.

grounding: A girl refuses to go anywhere with a stranger, keeps distance, tells the gate guard, then her parents.

subtype: Approach: going along because refusing feels rude [Pitfall]
passage: It was raining hard outside the tuition centre when a man stepped up to Vinita. "Your mother has had an accident. Come with me quickly." Vinita's stomach lurched. Her grandmother's rule rang in her ears: always listen to elders, never be rude. She followed him two lanes, her shoes soaked, though a small voice said, wait. At the corner, Vikas, the paan-shop owner who knew her family, called, "Vinita! Where are you going?" The man walked off fast. Vikas phoned her mother, who answered from home, perfectly well. Vinita was shaking. Later, drying her hair, she wondered why no one had told her that saying no was allowed too.

qa.q: Who called out to Vinita at the corner?
qa.a: Vikas, the paan-shop owner who knew her family, called out.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling as she followed the man?
qa.a: Frightened for her mother, and torn between the rule to obey elders and a small voice saying wait.

qa.q: What could Vinita do instead if a stranger says her mother is hurt, and why?
qa.a: She could refuse to go, stay near people and ask a trusted adult to phone her mother, because a real emergency can be checked without following a stranger.

qa.q: How does Vikas see the situation at the corner?
qa.a: Vikas sees a child from a family Vikas knows walking off with a stranger, so Vikas steps in and phones her mother.

grounding: A child taught to be polite to elders follows a stranger and is rescued, then sees safety must come before politeness.

subtype: Approach: noticing a mismatch in the story [Thinking]
passage: At the crowded bus stop, honking drowned half of what the man said. "I'm a friend of your uncle," he shouted, smiling. "He sent me to take you home." Uma looked at him. Her mother's brother, Chinmay Mama, had told her that anyone he sent would know the family word. "Which uncle? What's his name?" she asked. "The tall one... you know." "And the family word?" His smile stiffened. Uma took a step back, then another. "No thank you," she said, and moved toward the ticket counter, where a clerk watched the queue. The man turned away into the noise. Uma told the clerk everything. The clerk phoned Chinmay Mama and stayed with her until he came.

qa.q: What two things did Uma ask the man for?
qa.a: She asked his friend's name and the family word.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when the man could not give the family word?
qa.a: Uneasy and suspicious, since the story did not fit, so she stepped back and left.

qa.q: What else could Uma do if the man kept following her, and why?
qa.a: She could speak loudly and go closer to the clerk and the queue, because many people nearby make it easier to get help.

qa.q: How might the clerk see Uma's report?
qa.a: The clerk takes it seriously and sees a sensible child, so the clerk phones Chinmay Mama and stays with her.

grounding: A girl notices that a stranger claiming to know her uncle cannot give his name or the family word, and stays away.

subtype: Approach: family code word as a test [Action]
passage:
Papa had said it at breakfast: no word, no going.
"Yamini? Your father sent me to pick you up," the man said at the school gate.
Yamini stayed where she was. "What's the word?"
"The word?"
"Our family word. Only people Papa trusts know it."
"He didn't tell me any word. Come on, we'll be late."
"Then I'm not coming." She turned to the watchman. "Joseph Uncle, please call my father?"
"Fine, forget it," the man muttered, and walked off.
"Good girl," said Joseph Uncle. "Sit by my cabin. I'm calling him right now."

qa.q: Who does Yamini ask to call her father?
qa.a: She asks Joseph Uncle, the watchman.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when the man could not give the word?
qa.a: Wary and firm, since she refused to go and turned to the watchman for help.

qa.q: What else could Yamini's family add to keep pick-ups safe, and why?
qa.a: They could agree that Yamini phones her father to confirm any pick-up, which gives a second check besides the word.

qa.q: How does Joseph Uncle see Yamini's question about the word?
qa.a: Joseph Uncle sees a sensible child following a family plan, so he praises her and phones her father at once.

grounding: A family code word lets a girl test a man claiming her father sent him, and she leaves when he cannot give it.

subtype: Approach: helping in a safe way [Thinking]
passage: I was eating peanuts on the steps across from the bus stop when a car pulled up beside Pradeep, who was waiting for his bus. A woman in a hat leaned out holding a phone map. I couldn't hear her, but Pradeep stayed on the pavement, three big steps back, and called out, "The museum? Go straight, turn left at the big banyan tree, then it's next to the post office." He pointed with his whole arm. She thanked him and drove off. He never came closer, even when she waved the map at him. I don't know how he made up his mind so fast, but it looked like a good way to help. - Usha

qa.q: Where did Pradeep stand while he answered?
qa.a: He stayed on the pavement, three big steps back from the car.

qa.q: What might Pradeep have been thinking as he kept his distance?
qa.a: He probably wanted to be helpful but careful, choosing to help without going near the car.

qa.q: What other way could Pradeep help if the directions were hard to explain, and why?
qa.a: He could point out the post office or a shopkeeper who knows the road, since that helps without getting close to the car.

qa.q: How does Usha see Pradeep's answer?
qa.a: Usha thinks it looked like a good way to help, though Usha does not know how he decided so fast.

grounding: A boy asked for directions by a driver answers loudly from where he stands and points, without going near the car.

subtype: Approach: tempted by a gift or sweet [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday. Rekha Ma'am talked to Class Five about strangers. "A gift is never a reason to go anywhere with someone," she said. Zain doodled in his notebook.
Wednesday. After school a man at the lane offered him chocolate and a turn on a video game. "Just come and see something in the lane." Zain stared at the shiny wrapper and took a step. His friend Simran grabbed his sleeve. "Remember Monday? Come on!" They ran to the school gate.
Thursday. Zain told Rekha Ma'am, who wrote it all down and phoned his mother before lunch. He was still ashamed that he had nearly gone.

qa.q: Who grabbed Zain's sleeve in the lane?
qa.a: His friend Simran grabbed his sleeve.

qa.q: What was Zain feeling when he stared at the shiny wrapper?
qa.a: Tempted and eager for the treat, so his caution weakened and he took a step.

qa.q: What could Zain do next time he is offered a gift, and why?
qa.a: He could say no, step away and tell a trusted adult straight away, because a reward is not a reason to go anywhere.

qa.q: How does Simran see the offer in the lane?
qa.a: Simran recognises the situation Rekha Ma'am warned about and acts at once by pulling Zain away and running to the gate.

grounding: A boy tempted by a treat from a stranger takes a step, until his friend reminds him of the school safety talk.

subtype: Approach: telling a parent even when unsure [Revision]
passage: On the road home from the well, a stranger on a motorbike had asked Aditi to come along with him to see something. Her legs had locked, and she said nothing until he rode off. All evening at the village house she stirred the dal and kept quiet, ashamed that she had frozen. Then she went to Amma Sangeeta, who was folding clothes. "Something happened." Sangeeta set the clothes down and listened to all of it. "You did nothing wrong, Aditi. Thank you for telling me." They told her father that night, and her teacher the next morning. Now Aditi walks with a neighbour girl, and the family made a plan she could say by heart.

qa.q: Who did Aditi tell about what happened?
qa.a: Aditi told Amma Sangeeta.

qa.q: Why did Aditi keep quiet at first, and how did she feel?
qa.a: She felt ashamed that she had frozen, which is why she stirred the dal and said nothing all evening.

qa.q: What could Aditi do if a stranger asks her to come along again, and why?
qa.a: She could say no loudly, move toward people and tell an adult, as the family plan says, because telling early keeps more people watching out for her. 🤍

qa.q: How does Sangeeta respond to Aditi?
qa.a: Sangeeta puts down the clothes, listens to all of it, and tells Aditi she did nothing wrong, so Aditi feels heard rather than blamed.

grounding: A girl who froze in front of a stranger feels ashamed, then tells her mother, and the family adds a plan.

subtype: Approach: role-play practice of saying no loudly [Action]
passage: Sit down, children; I, Eshaan Sir, want to tell you about the safety practice we used to do at my school. Every Friday we made a game of it. One child played the stranger, and the others shouted "NO!" as loud as their chests would allow, then ran to me at the blackboard. Some of them giggled. Ritu, ten years old, giggled the most. Months later, at the fair, a man took hold of her sleeve and told her to come along. Ritu did not freeze. She shouted "NO!" so the whole lane turned, and ran to a shopkeeper. The practice had done the thinking for her legs.

qa.q: What did the children do in the Friday practice?
qa.a: One child played the stranger and the others shouted "NO!" as loud as they could, then ran to the teacher.

qa.q: What might Ritu have been feeling when the man took hold of her sleeve?
qa.a: Frightened, most likely, but the practice kept her from freezing.

qa.q: What choice did Ritu make at the fair, and why did it help?
qa.a: She shouted "NO!" so the whole lane turned and ran to a shopkeeper, and having practised made it a habit she could use.

qa.q: How does Eshaan Sir see the giggling during the practice?
qa.a: He seems to accept it as part of the game, since practice can be light and still work when it counts.

grounding: Children practise shouting no and running to a teacher, so a real situation brings a rehearsed response.
